title: Counting, Permutations and Combinations
objectives: Apply the multiplication principle to count multi-stage processes
Compute permutations $P(n,k)$ and combinations $C(n,k)$ and choose the right one for a scenario
Use complement counting for 'at least one' style questions
Compute probabilities of equally-likely outcomes by counting favourable and total cases
motivation: How many distinct equity option configurations does a desk have to price with 4 expiries, 5 strikes and 2 rights? How many 3-name baskets can you build from a 10-name universe, and what is the chance two dice (or two independent defaults) line up just wrong? Probability statements are almost always counting statements in disguise: count the outcomes you care about, divide by the outcomes possible. This lesson builds the two counting tools that every combinatorial probability question needs.

blocks.md: If a process happens in stages, and stage 1 has $n_1$ options, stage 2 has $n_2$ options regardless of what stage 1 chose, and so on, the whole process has $n_1 \times n_2 \times \cdots$ possible outcomes. Pricing 4 expiries $\times$ 5 strikes $\times$ 2 rights (call or put) means $4 \times 5 \times 2 = 40$ option configurations to cover. The twin rule handles alternatives: if you will do **either** task X (12 ways) **or** task Y (9 ways), never both, there are $12 + 9 = 21$ ways, **multiply** along a path, **add** across disjoint paths. Drawing the choice tree for small cases (3 expiries, 2 strikes: draw 6 leaves) keeps the principle honest before you trust it at scale.

blocks.caption: Two dice give 36 equally-likely pairs and 5 of them sum to 8, so the true probability is 5/36, watch the running frequency settle near 0.139.

blocks.md: A **permutation** is an arrangement in which order matters. The number of ways to pick $k$ items from $n$ distinct ones **in order** is $P(n,k) = \dfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}$, which is just the multiplication principle: $n$ choices for the first slot, $n-1$ for the second, ..., down to $n-k+1$. Ranking the top 3 of 8 job candidates gives $8 \times 7 \times 6 = 336$ orderings; listing all 8 in every possible order gives $8! = 40{,}320$. Note the same formula with $k = n$: a full shuffle of $n$ items is $n!$.

blocks.caption: Permutations: $n$ ways to fill slot one, $n-1$ slot two, ...

blocks.md: Selecting a **basket** of 3 stocks from 10 has no first, second or third place, the basket $\{A,B,C\}$ equals the basket $\{C,A,B\}$. Every unordered selection was counted $3! = 6$ times by the permutation formula (once per internal ordering), so we divide it out. That is the entire logic of the **combination** count:

blocks.caption: Combinations: permutations of $k$ ordered picks, divided by the $k!$ orderings that are the same selection.

blocks.md: So the 10-name universe offers $C(10,3) = \frac{10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8}{6} = 120$ baskets. Two identities you should be able to derive, not memorise: **symmetry** $C(n,k) = C(n, n-k)$ (choosing 3 to include equals choosing 7 to leave out, and indeed $C(10,3) = C(10,7) = 120$), and **Pascal's rule** $C(n,k) = C(n-1,\,k-1) + C(n-1,\,k)$, which counts selections by whether they contain a distinguished item.

rows: Pick 3 names for a basket from 10
Pick 2 of 5 desks to keep open

blocks.title: Worked example: a committee with a constraint
items: From 6 traders and 4 developers, form a 4-person committee containing **at least 2** developers.
Split by exact developer count (the cases are disjoint, so we add). Exactly 2 devs: $C(4,2) \cdot C(6,2) = 6 \times 15 = 90$.
Cross-check by complement: all committees $C(10,4) = 210$, minus 0 devs $C(6,4) = 15$, minus 1 dev $C(4,1) \cdot C(6,3) = 4 \times 20 = 80$: $210 - 15 - 80 = 115$. Both routes agree.

blocks.title: Combinatorial probability in one move
blocks.md: When outcomes are equally likely, $P(\text{event}) = \dfrac{\text{favourable}}{\text{total}}$. Five independent bonds each default with probability 0.1: the chance of **at least one** default is $1 - 0.9^5 \approx 0.4095$, because 'no default' is one countable outcome with probability $0.9^5$. 'At least one' questions are almost always easier backwards.

blocks.code:
from math import comb, perm
print(perm(8, 3))             # 336 - rank top 3 of 8
print(comb(10, 3))            # 120 - basket of 3 from 10
print(comb(10, 7))            # 120 - symmetry C(n,k) = C(n,n-k)
print(comb(4, 2) * comb(6, 2))  # 90  - committee: exactly 2 devs
blocks.caption: math.comb and math.perm (Python 3.8+) encode both formulas.

blocks.title: The overcounting reflex
blocks.md: Using $P(n,k)$ where a combination belongs overcounts by $k!$: treating a 3-name basket as an ordered list claims $720$ baskets instead of $120$. Ask one question before any formula: **would swapping two picks produce a different result?** If not, divide out the $k!$.

One more probability sample with real counting behind it: drawing 3 cards from a standard 52-card deck, the chance all three are hearts is $\dfrac{C(13,3)}{C(52,3)} = \dfrac{286}{22{,}100} \approx 0.0129$. The total $C(52,3)$ counts unordered hands, which is correct, because dealing order does not change the hand. Choosing $C$ over $P$ here is not a convention; it is the same 'would swapping change the outcome?' test.

guidedExercise.prompt: A screening committee of 4 must be formed from 6 quants and 3 salespeople, with **at least 2** salespeople on it. (1) Count the committees by splitting on the exact number of salespeople. (2) Verify your total by the complement method (total committees minus committees with 0 or 1 salespeople). (3) If the 4 chosen members are then randomly assigned to 4 named tasks, how many assignments exist per committee?
hints: Cases: exactly 2, exactly 3, exactly 4 salespeople, multiply $C(\text{sales}, i) \cdot C(\text{quants}, 4-i)$.
$C(9,4) = 126$ is the number of unrestricted committees.
Assigning 4 people to named tasks is a permutation, not a combination.
guidedExercise.solution: (1) Exactly 2 sales: $C(3,2) \cdot C(6,2) = 3 \times 15 = 45$. Exactly 3: $C(3,3) \cdot C(6,1) = 1 \times 6 = 6$. Exactly 4: $C(3,4) = 0$ (impossible). Total $= 51$. (2) Complement: $126 - C(6,4) - C(3,1) \cdot C(6,3) = 126 - 15 - 3 \times 20 = 126 - 15 - 60 = 51$. Agrees. (3) $4! = 24$ assignments per committee.

independentExercise.prompt: (1) Two fair dice are rolled once each. How many of the 36 outcomes give a sum of 8 or more? Hence what is $P(\text{sum} \ge 8)$? (2) Verify via the complement: how many outcomes give a sum of 7 or less, and do the two probabilities add to 1? (3) A fair coin is flipped 3 times. Use complement counting to find the probability of at least one head.
hints: Count outcomes per sum: there are 5 pairs summing to 8, then fewer for higher sums.
Sums 2 through 7 are the complement of sums 8 through 12.
'At least one head' fails only on the all-tails outcome.
independentExercise.solution: (1) Counts by sum: 8 has 5 pairs, 9 has 4, 10 has 3, 11 has 2, 12 has 1, total $5+4+3+2+1 = 15$, so $P = 15/36 = 5/12 \approx 0.4167$. (2) Sums 2-7 have $1+2+3+4+5+6 = 21$ outcomes, so $P(\text{sum} \le 7) = 21/36 = 7/12$; indeed $5/12 + 7/12 = 1$. (3) $P(\text{no heads}) = (1/2)^3 = 1/8$, so $P(\text{at least one head}) = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8$.

commonMistakes: Using permutations $P(n,k)$ for unordered selections, that overcounts by $k!$ (720 instead of 120 for a 3-name basket).
Adding $C(\text{A},i) \cdot C(\text{B},j)$ terms for cases that overlap instead of splitting on an exact count first.
Computing 'at least one' by summing 'exactly one', 'exactly two', ... instead of using $1 - P(\text{none})$.
Forgetting that $P = \text{favourable}/\text{total}$ assumes all outcomes are equally likely, it does not apply to biased or unequal-sized cases.
realWorldApplication: Feature-combination testing (which configs to run), A/B test group selection, network path enumeration and test-case design all reduce to permutations and combinations; getting the count right tells you the cost of exhaustive coverage before you run it.
quantFinanceApplication: Basket construction, pair-trading candidate sets, scenario grid sizes and default-correlation stress counts are all $C(n,k)$ values; the favourable-over-total method is exactly how closed-form probabilities for independent default pools are computed.
summary: Multiply along stages, add across disjoint alternatives: the multiplication principle is the root of every counting formula.
$P(n,k) = \frac{n!}{(n-k)!}$ for ordered selections; $C(n,k) = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$ for unordered ones, divide out $k!$ when order does not matter.
Constrained counts split into disjoint exact cases and add; verify hard ones by the complement method.
For equally-likely outcomes, probability is counting: $P = \text{favourable}/\text{total}$, and 'at least one' is $1 - P(\text{none})$.

quiz.prompt: How many ways can you choose 2 instruments from a watchlist of 9 (order irrelevant)?
A portfolio manager selects 5 stocks out of 30 for a new fund. Which expression gives the number of possible portfolios?
quiz.explanation: A portfolio is an unordered set of holdings, swapping two picks gives the same portfolio, so combinations apply: $C(30,5)$. $P(30,5)$ would count orderings 5! = 120 times over.

quiz.prompt: Compute $P(7,3)$: the number of ordered arrangements of 3 items chosen from 7.
What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
from math import comb
print(comb(6, 2) * comb(4, 2))
print(comb(10, 4))
quiz.explanation: $C(6,2) = 15$ and $C(4,2) = 6$, so the first line is $15 \times 6 = 90$ (choosing 2 from each group). $C(10,4) = 210$, the total number of 4-person committees from 10 people.

Symmetry gives $C(10,4) = C(10,6)$; the factorial form is the definition; Pascal's rule splits on whether item 10 is included. $10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 5040$ is $P(10,4)$ - missing the division by $4!$.

quiz.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is exactly 7? (Answer as a decimal.)

flashcards.back: $C(n,k) = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$ - use when order does not matter; satisfies $C(n,k) = C(n,n-k)$ and Pascal's rule.

flashcards.front: How do you decide permutation vs combination?
flashcards.back: Ask: would swapping two chosen items produce a different outcome? If yes, order matters (P); if no, divide out $k!$ (C).
Use the complement: $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none})$, since 'none' is usually a single countable outcome.
